A 45-year old HIV infected man presents to clinic. He has recently noticed some nodular lesions on his face and neck.
His last CD4 count three weeks ago was <100/mm. The lesion is biopsied and staining with Gomori's methanamine silver staindemonstrates the causative organism.
What is the appropriate treatment for this condition?
options: A long course of oral doxycycline
A long course of oral ﬂuconazole
explanation:
This patient has Cryptococcus neoformans skin lesions.
This is most often seen in T cell deﬁciency states and HIV-infected patients with CD4 counts of <100/mm.
Gomori's methanamine silver stain shows budding yeasts. Serum cryptococcal antigen can also be used in diagnosis.
Treatment is with an eight week course of ﬂuconazole 400 mg /day followed by 200 mg/day.
Chemotherapy is used in the management of Kaposi's sarcoma.
Topical ketoconazole is used to treat cutaneous candidiasis.
Topical corticosteroids may be used in drug eruptions secondary to highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART).

A 32-year-old lady of African origin presents to the HIV clinic. She has been known to the HIV service since coming to the UK 10 years ago.She currently takes tenofovir, emtricitabine and dolutegravir. She is extremely compliant with her current regime and is currently well.
She is 17 weeks pregnant and this is her ﬁrst pregnancy. Despite some vomiting earlier in the pregnancy, she is excited and feeling well.
Her blood tests show:
CD4 count0.84x10^9/L
CD8 count1.01x10^9/L
Viral load<20
She has come to discuss the management of her HIV with you.
What is the most appropriate management for this lady?
options: Continue current management and advise patient there is currently no reason why she should not have a vaginal delivery
Stop all HIV medications and advise this patient she will have to deliver by caesarean section
Continue the current medications, but at a lower dose so that the medications do not cross the placental barrier and effect the foetus
Stop this patient's current regime and change her onto zidovudine, lamivudine and nevirapine
Continue current regime and advise patient she will need to deliver by caesarean section to prevent transmission during birth
explanation:
It is recommended that women conceiving on an effective anti-retroviral (ART) regimen should continue this even if it containsefavirenz or does not contain zidovudine.
Exceptions are: (1) Protease inhibitor (PI) monotherapy should be intensiﬁed to include (depending on tolerability, resistance andprior antiretroviral history) one or more agents that cross the placenta. (2) The combination of stavudine and didanosine should notbe prescribed in pregnancy.
Although there is more evidence and experience in pregnancy with zidovudine plus lamivudine, tenofovir plus emtricitabine orabacavir plus lamivudine are acceptable nucleoside backbones. In the absence of speciﬁc contraindications, it is recommended thatthe third agent in ART should be efavirenz or nevirapine (if the CD4 cell count is less than 250 cells/ μ L) or a boosted PI.
No routine dose alterations are recommended for ARVs during pregnancy if used at adult licensed doses.

A 20-year-old man presents with dysuria and a urethral discharge. Gram staining of the urethral discharge demonstrates neutrophils but nobacteria.
Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
The most likely diagnosis is infection with Chlamydia trachomatis. Serovars D to K are the most common in the United Kingdom andpresent in men with urethritis, and in women with urethritis, cervicitis, salpingitis and consequent pelivic inﬂammatory disease.Affected women in particular may be asymptomatic. Chlamydia trachomatis is not visible with Gram stain.
Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1-3 and is endemic in Africa, India, the Caribbeanand South East Asia. It presents with a primary genital or skin lesion, followed by lymphadenopathy, ﬂu-like symptoms andoccasionally meningitis.
Escherichia coli is a common cause of urinary tract infections.
Treponema pallidum is the causative organism for syphilis.
Chlamydia psittici causes an atypical pneumonia in people exposed to respiratory secretions or aerosolised excreta from sick birds.

Following a diagnosis of Chlamydia trachomatis, a 24-year-old female patient presents with further questions about the diagnosis.
Which of the following is a recognised complication of Chlamydia trachomatis infection?
explanation:
Chlamydia trachomatis is the commonest sexually transmitted infection is the United Kingdom and is asymptomatic in 80% offemale patients.
Some of the complications of Chlamydia trachomatis are:Inclusion conjunctivitisOphthalmia neonatorumNon-speciﬁc urethritisProctitisCervicitisPelvic inﬂammatory diseasePeriappendicitis, andFitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome.
Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome is perihepatitis associated with Chlamydia trachomatis infection.
Pharyngitis is a complication of Chlamydia pneumoniae.
Psittacosis and ornithosis are caused by Chlamydia psittaci.

A 24-year-old builder presents to the Emergency department with a patch of erythema which is hot on the back of his hand. Within an hourthe erythema has spread up his arm and he is systemically unwell.
He is booked for urgent debridement in theatre.
Which antibiotics should be given, assuming no allergies?
explanation:
This is the classical presentation of necrotising fasciitis and it requires immediate surgical debridement. It is commonly caused bygroup A Streptococci and can be rapidly fatal.
Clindamycin binds to the 50S ribosomal subunit of rRNA and inhibits the initiation of peptide chain synthesis and is bacteriostatic. Itis also  a potent suppressor of bacterial toxin synthesis. Group A Streptocooci are usually very sensitive to benzylpenicillin so this isfrequently added though this does not neutralise the toxin.
Reference:
Kumar P, Clark M. Kumar and Clark Clinical Medicine. 6th ed. London: Saunders; 2005.

A 30-year-old male HIV positive patient is admitted with Pneumocystis jirovici pneumonia (PCP). He stopped taking co-trimoxazole therapythree weeks previously due to a rash.
Blood gases reveal:
pH 7.19 (7.36-7.44)
pCO5.3 kPa(4.7-6.0)
pO27.3 kPa(11.3-12.6)
Which of the following drug combinations would you select as treatment for this patient?
explanation:
This patient has severe PCP suggested by the pO2 below 10.
As he is allergic to co-trimoxazole alternative therapy would be IV pentamidine or clindamycin with primaquine.
Steroids have been shown to reduce mortality and prevent lung damage in people with moderate-to-severe PCP. (The severity isdetermined on the basis of arterial blood gas results.
These agents are used as adjunctive initial therapy only in patients with HIV infection who have severe PCP as deﬁned by a room airarterial oxygen pressure of less than 9 kPa (70 mmHg) or an arterial-alveolar O2 gradient that exceeds 4.5 kPa (35 mmHg).

A 18-year-old gentleman with T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia has been administered cytotoxic chemotherapy withcyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and corticosteroids (hyper-CVAD regimen).
On day 14 from starting chemotherapy the patient is noted to have a BP of 100/60 mmHg, a pulse rate of 120 bpm, a fever of 39°C withchills and rigors.
Which of the following will be your ﬁrst intervention in this case?
options: Blood and urine cultures and chest radiograph, together with C-reactive protein
Prompt administration of broad-spectrum antimicrobials to cover Gram negative and Gram positive organisms within minutes
Consideration for more intensive support on ITU
explanation:
This question covers the important topic of management of neutropenic sepsis.
Albeit management with ﬂuids, inotropes, culturing to discover the entity of the pathogen in every case are all important, the singlemost important intervention in neutropenic sepsis is the prompt institution of antimicrobial therapy, with broad-spectrumantimicrobials, for example, piperacillin/tazobactam and gentamicin.
Reference:
NICE. Neutropenic sepsis (CG151).

A 21-year-old medical student presents with a ten day history of fevers and malaise. There is no history of note.
On examination, he has enlarged lymph nodes palpable in both supraclavicular fossae. The nodes are smooth, mobile and non-tender. Thereis no recent history of overseas travel. He returned from his elective period in Gambia three months previously.
His blood ﬁlm is shown below:

explanation:
The blood ﬁlm shows typical trypomastigotes of African trypanosomiasis.
The causative agent is Trypanosoma brucei and is transmitted to humans by the bite of the tsetse ﬂy.

A 45-year-old man presents with acute onset of scrotal swelling and dysuria.
On examination there is unilateral tenderness, erythema, and swelling of the scrotum. The patient denies any recent history of trauma. Hehas however had recurrent episodes of urinary tract infections.
What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
options: Ultrasound scan of scrotum and surgical review
Urinary cultures, empirical antibiotics and bed rest
Start treatment to cover Chlamydia and gonorrhoea
Insert urethral catheter and commence trimethoprim
explanation:
This patient has epididymitis.
The most common pathogens in men over the age of 35 are coliforms and Pseudomonas.
The presence of long term catheters, underlying urinary tract pathology or recent instrumentation are risk factors for epididymitis.
The most appropriate immediate management is to commence empirical antibiotics which cover Gram positive and negativeorganisms while awaiting urinary cultures, scrotal elevation, bed rest, and analgesia.
Topical steroids have no role in the management of epididymitis.
Torsion is characteristically associated with younger males and less so in adults, though of course it is always kept on the differential.
Epididymitis is associated with frequent urinary tract infections, which is a clue in the question.

A 23-year-old student is referred by his G.P for investigation of a six month history of malaise, anorexia, and weight loss. He also describes afour week history of diarrhoea.
On examination he is cachectic. On inspection of his oral mucosae he has white frond-like patches on both lateral margins of his tongue.Attempts to scrape off the patches are unsuccessful.
What is the causative organism of the abnormality on his tongue?
explanation:
This describes oral hairy leukoplakia, a condition seen in HIV-infected patients with a CD4 count between 200 and 500/mm.
The condition is painless, however, unlike Candida, the lesions cannot be scraped off the tongue.
The diagnosis is a clinical one. As it is asymptomatic, treatment is rarely required.
The condition responds to highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART).
Human herpes virus 8 (HHV8) is the causative organism for Kaposi's sarcoma.
Tinea rubrum causes fungal skin and nail infections.

A 19-year-old male student attends the Emergency department complaining of an urethral discharge one week after having casualunprotected sex.
Gram stain shows numerous neutrophils, some of which contain Gram negative intracellular Diplococci. The patient is treated withceftriaxone, 250 mg as an intramuscular injection. Five days later, the patient re-attends with persisting discharge.
Which of the following is the most likely cause of this discharge?
explanation:
Gonorrhoea is one of the commonest reported STDs in both men and women. In men the symptoms manifest as urethritis and inwomen cervicitis or urethritis.
This patient has been adequately treated for gonorrhoea and a persistent discharge would be unusual unless there is antibioticresistance in which case a culture assay will help to determine sensitivities.
More commonly patients present with co-infection with Chlamydia trachomatis.
In this case the patient is likely to have a non-speciﬁc urethritis (NSU) due to Chlamydia trachomatis, requiring treatment with eitherdoxycycline or erythromycin for 7-14 days.

An 89-year-old woman presents to the emergency room with increased shortness of breath and decreased mobility of 1-week duration. Hershortness of breath is worse at night and she sometimes wakes up gasping for breath. She has fallen over twice in the last week which is notnormal for her.
She has a past medical history of diabetes mellitus type 2 and hypertension. She has had no previous surgeries. She lives independently withher husband and her daughter lives close by and helps with the shopping.
On examination, she is found to have coarse crackles bi-basally on auscultation of her chest. She has a regular heart rate with a pan-systolicmurmur loudest over the apex.
Investigations show: CXR - bilateral blunting of the costophrenic angles and upper lobe diversionHaemoglobin  11g/dl, WCC  6 x 10^9/l ,Platelets  178 x 10^9/lSodium 139 mmol/l Potassium  4.2 mmol/l, Urea  8 mmol/l, Creatinine  92 mol/lBlood cultures - Methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureusEchocardiogram - Severe mitral regurgitation with large mobile structure on valve leaﬂet
What is the best treatment option for this lady?
options: Amoxicillin 1 g IV three times daily and Vancomycin 250mg IV twice daily
Flucloxacillin 2 g IV six times daily
Flucloxacillin 1 g IV four times daily
Amoxicillin 1 g IV three times daily and Vancomycin 120mg IV three times daily
explanation:
This lady has a native mitral valve endocarditis with a bacteraemia caused by a methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus Aureus. Oncecultures have grown the causative bacteria and it is found to be sensitive to methicillin guidelines suggest Flucloxacillin 2 g IV sixtimes daily to be the treatment of choice. There is some debate about optimal length of treatment, but 6 weeks of intravenoustherapy is generally accepted as the length of treatment needed. Shorter therapeutic regimens may be effective in selected patientswith right-sided endocarditis and with endocarditis due to highly susceptible viridans streptococci treated with synergisticantimicrobials.

A 30-year-old HIV positive patient presents to the emergency department. His most recent CD4 count was 100 (1000-1500).
His presenting complaint is of a gradual onset of mild generalised headache and fever. He has had one episode of vomiting. On physicalexamination, he is febrile with a temperature of 38°C. He has no photophobia or papilloedema. There is mild nuchal rigidity.
Bearing in mind the most likely diagnosis, what is the appropriate treatment to commence following a diagnostic lumbar puncture?
explanation:
It is likely that this patient has Cryptococcus meningo-encephalitis. The causative organism is Cryptococcus neoformans, a funguswhich causes severe infection in patients with defective cell-mediated immunity.
This is an AIDS-deﬁning illness which typically occurs when the CD4 count is less than or below 100. Symptoms are typically ofgradual onset over one to two weeks. Diagnosis is by examination of CSF with India ink. This will demonstrate typical encapsulatedyeast forms.
Treatment regimes include the use of IV amphotericin B, to which ﬂucytosine is sometimes added. In certain instances a long courseof ﬂuconazole may be used.

Of note, he had undergone splenectomy 20 years previously after he suffered splenic rupture in a road traﬃc accident.
On examination his left knee appeared swollen and was hot to touch. Aspirate of the joint was sent for microscopy. Gram stain of the aspirateis shown below.
 
 
What is the causative organism?
explanation: The Gram stain shows Gram positive cocci growing in clusters, typical of Staphylococcus aureus.

Four weeks after his return he presents to the emergency department with an eight week history of myalgia, weakness and an undulantfever.
Blood tests results are as follows:

explanation: Brucellosis is a zoonotic infection caused by Brucella which can be found in infected farm animals in endemic areas such as theMediterranean basin, central and South America and South East Asia.

A 38-year-old man presents to you with fever and tiredness. He has returned from a holiday to Costa Maya, Mexico two weeks ago. There isno history of cough, diarrhoea, or vomiting and no known infectious contacts.
On examination, his blood pressure is 140/98 and heart rate 52/min. You strongly suspect this to be Salmonella typhi.
Which of the following oral antibiotics would be most suitable to commence treatment?
explanation:
Fluoroquinolones reach an excellent intracellular concentration and if the organism is fully susceptible, remain the drug of choice.Resistance to ﬂuoroquinolones is developing in South Asia, where the drug to consider would be Azithromycin.
Ceftriaxone is a parenteral antibiotic and not an oral preparation.
Ampicillin, chloramphenicol and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole are all outdated due to resistance, and should not be used withoutconﬁrmed sensitivities.

A 24-year-old woman consults her general practitioner with a one day history of fever and a macular rash. She is eight weeks pregnant andhas not been immunised against rubella.
Her GP refers her to the hospital for further advice after obtaining blood test results that showed negative rubella IgM and a rubellahaemagglutination inhibition (HAI) titre of 1:64.
What advice do you give the patient?
options: Give the patient a rubella vaccination
Ask the patient to return one week later to repeat the test
Tell the patient that she has rubella and advise on the possible risk to her fetus
Refer the patient for termination of pregnancy
Reassure the patient that she does not have rubella
explanation:
A positive rubella haemagglutination inhibition (HAI) combined with a negative rubella IgM is consistent with:Early acute infection with rubellaPrevious vaccination, orPrevious rubella infection.
The most important issue to resolve is whether she has acute rubella.
The IgM may take several days to rise and the test should be repeated one to two weeks later.

You are called to review a 60-year-old alcoholic with multiple abscesses.
As the patient is put on empirical antibiotics a pus sample is taken to the laboratory. The laboratory report is partially written but says thereare Gram positive organisms, in irregular clusters, catalase and coagulase positive.
What is the causative agent for the boils?
explanation:
Staphylococcus aureus is Gram positive, in irregular clusters, produces catalase and coagulase.
Micrococcus is the wrong option. These are rarely pathologic, they are just skin contaminates.
Neisseria gonococcus is the wrong option because it is a Gram negative coccus.
Staphylococcus albus is the wrong option because despite its being Gram positive and producing catalase it does not producecoagulase.
Streptococcus pyogenes is the wrong option because it is Gram positive in chains and does not produce catalase.

A 30-year-old woman presents with a rash on her upper thighs.
She ﬁrst noticed the rash three days ago and describes it as itchy and red. She also describes itchy hands. She lives with her partner and 3-year-old son and works as a care assistant in a nursing home.
On examination she has a dry erythematous papular rash on the medial aspect of both thighs.
Which of the following is the appropriate treatment for the most likely condition?
explanation:
This patient has scabies.
Scabies is caused by Sarcoptes scabiei; it is an infestation of the skin that is most often seen as outbreaks in institutions such asnursing homes and schools. After fertilisation the female mite burrows into the skin and leaves behind a trail of about 40 eggs.Burrowing mites cause intense itching usually in the folds of skin between the ﬁngers, ﬂexor wrist surfaces, the abdomen and thighs.
Diagnosis is by microscopic examination of the mite, its faeces or eggs.
The entire household will require treatment with malathion 0.5% liquid.

This 28-year-old man presented with a painful red eye.
He had previously been well. He reported having two episodes of shingles in the past two years.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The slide shows Kaposi's sarcoma (KS) of the eye. The lesion is a red-purple mass arising from the conjunctiva. It is not limited to thesclera (which could suggest a subconjunctival haemorrhage) and it protrudes, which also favours a malignant growth. Eyelid wouldbe an unusual area for a melanoma and it would not be expected to be quite so erythematous, perfused, or superﬁcially spreading.NHL does not tend to present with superﬁcial deposits. A stye (or meibomian gland cyst) is a swelling on the eyelid and does notextend onto the eyeball.

A 14-year-old girl presented to hospital with a 24 hour history of nausea, vomiting and abdominal cramps.
On examination, she was afebrile but had a tender abdomen with guarding. Three hours after administration of a speciﬁc agent, she passed alarge quantity of material in her stools (pictured).
What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Ascaris lumbricoides is a large roundworm, growing up to 35 cm in length, and is the most common nematode parasite of humans.Infected patients are often asymptomatic. Symptoms may develop as a result of pneumonitis caused by the worm's migrationthrough the lungs, obstruction of the gastrointestinal tract or biliary/pancreatic duct obstruction. Piperazine is the treatment ofchoice in patients presenting with bowel obstruction; mebendazole may be used to treat other infections.
Strongyloides stercoralis is a nematode infection. Symptoms may be cutaneous (pruritus due to invasion by the nematodes),pulmonary (eosinophilic pneumonia due to passage through the lungs) or gastrointestinal (abdominal pain).

A 62-year-old male is being discharged from hospital after being treated for pneumonia.
All the clinical signs and symptoms are normal on discharge, but he is a smoker.
When would you like to review him and his chest radiograph after discharge?
explanation:
Due to the age of the patient and the fact that he is a smoker it is necessary to do a review of the chest radiograph to make sure thatit is not cancer. There is also a need to get know whether the patient is thinking about smoking cessation and how he is dealing withit.
After one week will be too early to see any radiographic changes.
After two weeks is the wrong option because some studies have shown that 51% of chest radiographs would have shown changes.
After four weeks is the wrong option because some studies show that 61% of the radiographs would have shown some changescompared to six weeks where up to 73% will be showing changes.
Never is the wrong option; given his age and the history of smoking he should be reviewed to rule out cancer and to help him quitsmoking.

A 24-year-old man presented with increasing shortness of breath on exertion. He had been unwell for over two weeks with intermittentfevers and chills. Over the two days preceding his admission to hospital he had developed breathlessness on minimal exertion with a coughproductive of blood-stained sputum.
He had no previous hospital admissions. He was unemployed and had been homeless until three months previously. He lived in a ﬂat with hisgirlfriend and their dog. He admitted to regular use of recreational drugs and occasionally injected intravenously.
On examination he was febrile 38.5°C. His jugular venous pressure was 9 cm above the sternal angle when lying supine at 45°. His bloodpressure was 100/60 mmHg with pulse 104 beats per minute. A pansystolic murmur was audible at the lower left sternal edge.
The chest radiograph showed multiple opacities throughout both lung ﬁelds.
Which of the following antimicrobial regimes is most likely to be effective in treating this patient?
explanation:
This patient has signs and symptoms of right heart endocarditis indicating an urgent need for antibiotics. It is likely that infection hasbeen acquired as a result of intravenous drug use using dirty needles or equipment.
The causative organism in most cases of endocarditis from IV use is Staphylococcus aureus.
The combination of vancomycin and gentamicin is the only one of the options that would provide adequate antibacterial cover. Thiscombination would also cover MRSA. Some clinicians would use ﬂucloxacillin plus gentamicin as the combination of ﬁrst choice insuch a patient, but since this is not an option this information is of academic interest only.
IVDUs are also at risk of developing fungal endocarditis (most frequently non-albicans Candida sp), though this is less common thanStaphylococcus aureus.
Empiric therapy should start with anti-staphylococcal therapy, as outlined above. If the patient fails to respond or other organismsare isolated from culture specimens, then a change of antibiotic therapy should be made.

stem: What is the commonest cause for this appearance?
explanation:
The slide shows typical target lesions of erythema multiforme (EM).
Herpes simplex virus infection is the commonest cause. Other common causes include infection with Mycoplasma andStreptococci.
EM may also:Be idiopathicBe drug-induced (sulfonamides, sulphonylureas, barbiturates)Occur in systemic diseases (SLE, inﬂammatory bowel disease, malignancy).

stem: What organism has been cultured from a sputum sample from a 16-year-old girl with a chronic cough and diarrhoea?
explanation:
The culture plate shows a growth of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, characterised by the green colouration of the colonies due toproduction of the pigment pyocyanin.
The history is consistent with a diagnosis of cystic ﬁbrosis; bronchiectasis associated with CF frequently results in recurrentinfections with Pseudomonas.

Bactericidal antibiotics should be used to treat infections of the endocardium and meninges if possible.
Host defences are relatively ineffective at these sites and the dangers imposed by such infections require prompt eradication of theseorganisms.
Which of these antibiotics is bactericidal?
explanation: Gentamicin is bactericidal and the other options are bacteriostatic.

You have a 30-year-old male patient.
He is HIV positive and his CD4+ is 300 cells/mm He is eager to travel to the central Americas for a business trip.
Which of these live vaccines can you safely give him?
explanation:
Despite its being a live vaccine the yellow fever vaccine is safe, especially if the patient's CD4+ is above 200 cells/mm.
BCG vaccine (tuberculosis) eﬃcacy is doubted and there is a high chance of getting BCGitis.
Inﬂuenza vaccine (intranasal) is not safe and there are safe alternatives.
Oral polio vaccine (OPV) is not safe and there is a safe alternative, the inactivated polio vaccine.
Typhoid vaccine (Ty21a) is wrong and there are safe alternatives.

This HIV positive man presented with cough, haemoptysis and a rash.
What is the causative agent of the skin lesions?
explanation:
The picture shows characteristic purple lesions of Kaposi's sarcoma (KS); the most common variant of KS is seen in patients with HIV.
In HIV infection, KS lesions occur most commonly on the face; however lesions may be widely disseminated in skin, bronchial treeand gastrointestinal tract.
Pulmonary disease can present with dyspnoea and cough with haemoptyis; it is usually associated with cutaneous disease, but canpresent in isolation. Chest x ray may show pulmonary nodules.
KS is caused by human herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8) infection.

A 26-year-old woman presents and complains of a thin, white ﬁshy-smelling discharge which is most noticeable after intercourse.
Saline wet mount reveals the presence of clue cells.
What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Clue cells on saline wet mount are the best predictors of bacterial vaginosis.
Trichomoniasis and atrophic vaginosis are characterised by dyspareunia and inﬂammation which are absent in bacterial vaginosis.
Infection resolves spontaneously in one-third of cases. Treatment regimes include a seven day course of metronidazole orclindamycin.

In retinitis due to Toxocara canis, there is usually only a single, well demarcated lesion.
Rare helminthic presentation. Toxocara canis are live in the digestive systems of dogs.
More common in children than adults.

A 34-year-old gentleman presents with sudden onset fever, pharyngitis, myalgia anddiarrhoea. He has no relevant past medical history except for having travelled through SierraLeone two weeks ago. He has otherwise been well.
On examination he looked unwell and his temperature was 38°C. There were no signs of haemorrhage or rash. His chest, abdominal andneurological examinations were intact.
He had a slight thrombocytopaenia but otherwise the full blood count (FBC) was unremarkable. He had mild dehydration biochemically andthe liver function tests were otherwise normal.
Which of the following options is the most likely diagnosis?

A 22-year-old female student presents with generalised pruritus of six weeks duration.
She has little other history of note and has otherwise been well. This itching has deteriorated over this time and is particularly worse at night.She has been unaware of any rashes and denies taking any prescribed drugs. There is no history of atopy.
She shares a ﬂat with her boyfriend and drinks approximately 12 units per week and smokes cannabis occasionally.
On examination, there is little of note except there are some scratch marks over the shoulders and back and she has some erythemabetween the ﬁngers. Otherwise cardiovascular, respiratory and abdominal examination is normal.
Which of the following therapies would be most appropriate treatment for this patient?
explanation:
This patient has scabies, a highly contagious disease caused by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei, and is quite common in the sexuallyactive.
It is well recognised to cause generalised pruritus and one should make a careful examination between the ﬁnger spaces forburrows.
Appropriate treatment includes permethrin cream, topical benzyl benzoate, and malathion. The permethrin cream doesn't have anydirect effect on the pruritis itself but helps to settle symptoms indirectly by killing the mite, which is the root cause. You shouldcounsel your patients that it may take longer for the itching to settle as the allergic reaction to the mite abates and that the creamshould be appplied everywhere below the neck, not merely where there is rash present.
References:
British National Formulary: Permethrin
BMJ Best Practice: Scabies
Primary Care Dermatology Society: Scabies

A 47-year-old Asian man has a Mantoux test performed as part of an immigration screen on entry into the United Kingdom.
The test proves to be positive, but his chest radiograph is normal, and he is started on isoniazid and pyridoxine (vitamin B). Four weeks laterhe presents to hospital with fever, abdominal pain and jaundice.
What is the most likely explanation for his symptoms?
explanation:
Isoniazid monotherapy is used for prevention of active TB in individuals with proven exposure to M. tuberculosis.
Isoniazid-induced hepatitis occurs in ~1% of individuals and is much commoner in people more than 35-years-old (risk of hepatitis isless than 0.3% in patients under 20 years; 2-3% risk in individuals over 50 years).
Other side effects of isoniazid therapy include peripheral neuritis (pyridoxine given prophylactically) and a systemic lupuserythematosus (SLE)-like syndrome.

A 78-year-old male comes to your practice with a cough of one week's duration, diﬃculty in breathing, chest pain, chills and sweats.
On examination he is in a fairly good general condition. He has a temperature of 38°C and BP 110/70 mmHg. His respiratory rate is 28breaths/minute.
On auscultation he has some crepitations. He has a urea of 4.5 mmol/l (2.5 - 7.5 mmol/L).
He seems to have a band which shows he is allergic to penicillin.
How would you treat this patient?
options: Oral levoﬂoxacin 500 mg od for ﬁve days
Oral doxycycline 100 mg od plus oral clarithromycin 500 mg bd for ﬁve days
Oral doxycycline 200 mg loading then 100 mg od for one week
IV ceftriaxone 2 g od plus IV clarithromycin
explanation:
The patient has a CURB-65 score of 1, so he has pneumonia of very low severity. Since he is allergic to penicillin, doxycycline alonewill be effective in the treatment of pneumonia in this particular case.
IV ceftriaxone 2 g od plus IV clarithromycin 500 mg bd would be effective but unnecessary. This combination is used to treat highseverity pneumonia.
IV ceftriaxone 2 g od is the wrong answer. The patient has low severity pneumonia so there is no need to use an intravenous routefor treatment.
Oral levoﬂoxacin 500 mg od for ﬁve days could be effective but it is unnecessary. It is used to treat moderate severity pneumonia.
Oral doxycycline 100 mg od plus oral clarithromycin 500 mg bd for ﬁve days could be effective but is unnecessary. It is used to treatmoderate severity pneumonia.

This thoracic CT scan was performed on a Brazilian male who presented with dysphagia.
What is the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
The slide shows a chagasic megaoesophagus: a massively dilated oesophagus containing both food residue and radio-opaquecontrast medium.
Chagas' disease is caused by T. cruzi, which infects humans via a bloodsucking insect vector (triatomine bugs).
Treponema pallidum is a spirochaete which causes syphilis.
Mycobacterium tuberculosis is an acid-fast bacillus, the most common and well-known Mycobacterium.

A 45-year-old woman of African descent is brought to your practice with a history of having been treated for pulmonary tuberculosis for twoweeks with RHZE.
Her HIV serology is positive:
CD4+ 50 cells/mm
Creatinine clearance (CrCl)40 mg/m
ALT 28 mg/dL
AST 26 mg/dL
On examination the patient is wasted, slightly anaemic with an Hb 80 g/L. The rest of the ﬁndings are not very signiﬁcant.
What HAART regimen would you use for this patient?
explanation:
Efavirenz is used in combination with an NRTIs because it has little effect on the plasma levels of rifampin which is being used totreat the pulmonary tuberculosis. The combination of abacavir/emtricibine is chosen for this given case because of the lowcreatinine clearance which is below 50 mg/m.The use of tenofovir is likely to cause nephrotoxicity.
Stavudine/lamivudine/efavirenz is the wrong option because dideoxythymidine (D4T) has a very high toxicity proﬁle. Most countrieshave stopped using it unless there is no other option or for children less than 5 where it is not very toxic. It is likely to causemitochondria toxicity and lipodystrophy among others.
Tenofovir/emtricitabine/efavirenz is the wrong option because the creatinine clearance is below 50 mg/mm. There is a high
likelihood of nephrotoxicity if TDF is used.

A 24-year-old man with chronic renal failure underwent renal transplantation with a matched related donor graft.
The immediate post-operative period was uneventful and he was discharged home after two weeks with a fully-functioning graft. One monthlater he presented to the nephrology clinic with a high fever and he was admitted for further investigations.
His full blood count showed a marked leukopenia. During the ﬁrst evening of his admission, his clinical condition deteriorated rapidly and hebecame dyspnoeic. On reviewing the other investigations, his liver function tests were noted to be markedly deranged.
Which of the following is the most likely cause of his illness?
explanation:
Cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection is responsible for a substantial fraction of the morbidity and mortality following organtransplantation.
Two main factors determine whether a patient will develop CMV infection after transplantation :1. Whether the donor or recipient harbours a latent virus capable of reactivation after transplantation2. The degree of immunosuppression after transplantation.
Primary disease is the commonest and most severe type of post-transplant CMV infection. This occurs in individuals who have neverbeen infected with CMV who receive an allograft that contains latent virus from a CMV-seropositive donor.

What is the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
Ascending cellulitis is shown.
Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococci are the commonest causative organisms.

stem:
You are an infectious disease expert with the World Health Organisation.
Guidelines on the ﬁrst line treatment of severe malaria are being updated but expert opinion is divided over the recommendation of a newdrug.
What type of study would you undertake?
explanation:
It is important to be aware of the different types of study design and when a particular study should be used.
In this instance an RCT would be the most appropriate. RCT is the gold standard for evaluation of eﬃcacy for therapeutic andpreventative measures. It would be the best choice here to enable an informed decision on choice of drug.
A case-control study is retrospective and is one that selects participants who have a particular condition or disease (cases) alongwith participants who do not have that particular condition or disease (controls). Information on past exposures among cases iscompared with information on past exposures among controls. This study design is important for rare diseases. Case-control studiesare used to generate hypotheses.
Case series describe the experience of a single patient (report) or a group (series) of patients with similar diagnoses orcharacteristics. Cases are usually identiﬁed over a relatively short period of time. They identify the beginning of an epidemic, a newdisease, or previously unobserved exposure-disease relation.
A cohort study is prospective and is an epidemiologic study design in which the incidence of a disease (or condition) is comparedamong exposed and unexposed individuals. It provides information on etiology of disease, as well as the natural history of diseaseand survival of those with disease.
Cross sectional studies are prevalence studies and take a "snap-shot" of a disease at a single point in time. They are used to ﬁnd theprevalence of disease. They will not be helpful in informing us about eﬃcacy of a drug.

In many hospitals, 40%-50% of the S. aureus isolates are resistant to methicillin.
What is the basis of methicillin resistance in Staphylococci?
options: Impaired penetration of drug target penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs)
explanation:
The resistant organisms produce PBPs that have a low aﬃnity for binding beta-lactamase antibiotics. Other organisms which do thesame are Pneumococci and Enterococci.
Eﬄux is the wrong option.
Inactivation of antibiotic by beta-lactamase is wrong for the case of MRSA, but it is used by some for S. aureus, Haemophilus sp, andEscherichia coli.
Impaired penetration of drug target penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) is wrong as it occurs often in Gram negative bacteria becauseof their impermeable cell membrane.
Replacement of a sensitive pathway is the wrong option.

stem: Which of the following agents is the most appropriate to treat this lesion?
explanation:
Dendritic ulcers are caused by herpes simplex virus.
Presentation is usually with pain, photophobia, blurred vision, conjunctivitis and chemosis.
Steroid eye drops are contraindicated as they may induce massive amoeboid ulceration and blindness.
They are treated with aciclovir eye drops, which should be continued for three days after the ulcer has healed.

stem:
A 64-year-old man presents with a two month history of confusion. There is no previous history of cardiovascular or peripheral vasculardisease. He denies any fever or meningism.
On examination he was afebrile. Neurological examination demonstrated an ataxic gait and reduced coordination.
Which of the following tests is the most appropriate to help make the diagnosis of tertiary syphilis?
options: Spinal ﬂuid culture to grow the organism
explanation:
Tertiary syphilis presents up to 20 years after the primary infection and can affect:The mucous membranes (gummatous syphilis)The cardiovascular system (cardiovascular syphilis), andThe neurological system (late neurosyphilis).
Venereal Disease Research Laboratory test (VDRL) detects antibodies to cardiolipin, which is produced as a response to treponemalinfection. It is very sensitive in early infection but sensitivity declines in late-stage infection. It is not speciﬁc and may also give falsenegative results in HIV co-infection.
Treponema pallidum haemagglutination test (TPHA) uses speciﬁc treponemal antigens and therefore are more speciﬁc. Both VDRLand TPHA are often positive in gummatous syphilis. However in cardiovascular and neurosyphilis, TPHA is positive and VDRL is oftennegative.
Culture is expensive and time consuming and is rarely used in diagnosis. Spinal ﬂuid samples may demonstrate a positive VDRL, lowglucose and raised protein, however results are variable.

stem:
A 40-year-old company executive went to Mexico for a four day business trip.
Five days after her return to the United Kingdom she is said to have got a fever, headache, pains at the back of the eyes, back pain and severemuscle pain. She reports development of a rash of late which started on the trunk and spread to the extremities and the face.
On examination she is ill-looking. Her temperature is 38°C and BP 120/70 mmHg. She has a scleral injection. Her adenoids are swollen withpalatal vesicles. The patient has a maculopapular rash all over her body.
What tests would you do to conﬁrm the diagnosis?
explanation:
Most of the viruses spread by rodents and arthropods cause similar symptoms and signs, but the case above is dengue fever which isdiagnosed by dengue fever serology.
Dengue fever has an incubation period of two to seven days. The patient often experiences a sudden onset of fever, headache, andretro-orbital pain and back pains with severe myalgia hence the name breakbone fever.
There is often adenopathy, palatal vesicles and sclera injection on the ﬁrst day. There may be anorexia, nausea or vomiting. When thepatient is near recovery there may develop a maculopapular rash beginning on the trunk and spreading to the extremities and theface. Epistaxis and scattered petechiae may be observed.
Thin and thick blood slides will rule out some diseases like malaria. The incubation period for malaria is about seven to 21 days butmay go as far as six months. The patient is more likely to have a fever, headache, back pain and myalgia but rarely a maculopapularrash, adenopathy, palatal vesicles and sclera injection.
Blood cultures could be used to rule out mainly bacterial infections.
HIV serology is the wrong option. HIV especially the acute HIV disease presents like an upper respiratory tract infection. It could beconfused with dengue fever hence the need to rule it out.
Stool microscopy and culture is the wrong option.

A 55-year-old man is brought to the Emergency department with a two week history of fever, chills and malaise.
On physical examination abnormal ﬁndings include bilateral conjunctival haemorrhages, splenomegaly with a pansystolic murmur consistentwith mitral regurgitation. Infective endocarditis is suspected. No antibiotics have been given so far.
How should the blood samples be drawn to maximise the chances of obtaining positive cultures?
options: Draw three samples of blood from different venepuncture sites with the ﬁrst separated from the last by at least one hour over 24 hours
Draw three blood samples from the cubital fossa each one hour apart from the next but within the ﬁrst 24 hours at the peak of a fever
Draw two blood samples from different venepuncture sites with the ﬁrst separated from the last by at least one hour collected over 24hours.
Draw two samples of blood from different venepuncture sites each one hour apart from the next but within the ﬁrst 24 hours
Draw three samples of blood from different venepuncture sites each one hour apart from the next but within the ﬁrst 24 hours
explanation:
Blood culture is important in infective endocarditis; it is an important aid in making the diagnosis and the treatment.
How the sample is drawn helps with the ﬁnal result. The ESC guidelines are the point of reference for this procedure.
Further Reading:1. Beynon RP, Bahl VK, Prendergast BD. Infective endocarditis. BMJ. 2006;333:334-9.2. Habib G, Hoen B, Tornos P, et al. Guidelines on the prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of infective endocarditis (new version2009). Eur Heart J. 2009;30:2369-413.3. Li JS, Sexton DJ, Mick N, et al. Proposed modiﬁcations to the Duke criteria for the diagnosis of infective endocarditis. Clin InfectDis. 2000;30:633-8.

He had initially presented six months previously with Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia with a CD4 T lymphocyte count of 10 cells/mm andhad subsequently started on highly active antiretroviral therapy. His most recent CD4 count, taken one month prior to his new presentation,was 50 cells/mm.
On examination he has no focal weakness, but both plantar responses are extensor. Fundoscopy is normal.
A CT scan of his brain is shown.
What is the diagnosis?

A 56-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of dysuria with localised tingling of the genitalia, and shooting pains.
Which of the following is true regarding genital herpes?
options: Most primary cases present with symptoms
Transmission can occur in the absence of lesions
Recurrent episodes tend to be more severe
It is most commonly secondary to herpes simplex virus-1 infection
Topical aciclovir is the treatment of choice
explanation:
Genital herpes is most commonly caused by herpes simplex virus-2 (HSV).
Sixty per cent of primary cases are asymptomatic.
Recurrent attacks tend to be shorter and less severe.
Viral shedding can occur in the absence of lesions.
Antiviral treatment reduces the severity of episodes but is not curative.
Topical aciclovir is of little beneﬁt.

stem:
An 82-year-old lady was admitted to hospital with fever and confusion. She had been found collapsed at home by her son, who reported thatshe was usually ﬁt and well and coped well on her own at home.
She had a past history of angina, which was well-controlled on a beta-blocker and oral nitrate and she also suffered from osteoarthritis.
On examination she looked pale and unwell and smelled strongly of stale urine. Her temperature was 38.1°C. She was disoriented in time,place and person. Her blood pressure was 80/45 mmHg with pulse 110 beats per minute and regular.
There were widespread petechiae on the limbs. Her respiratory rate was measured at 28 breaths per minute. Her heart sounds were normaland the chest clear. Her abdomen was soft, but she was very tender in the suprapubic region and a mass was felt rising from the pelvic brim.
After taking blood, it was noted that there was continued bleeding from the venous puncture site. A urinary catheter was inserted andyielded 1500 ml of cloudy yellow offensive-smelling urine.
Which of the following statements is true?
options: Circulating levels of activated protein C (aPC) will be reduced
Levels of ﬁbrin degradation products (FDPs) will be reduced
The platelet count is likely to be elevated
Levels of D-dimer will be reduced
The activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) will be below the normal range
explanation: The patient has disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) secondary to sepsis. Given the history, the most likely source is theurinary tract.

A 42-year-old man, recently diagnosed with HIV, wants to travel around the world andpresents to clinic with inquiries about the necessary vaccinations.
His most recent CD4 count is 190; however he does not wish to commence highly active anti-retroviral therapy (HAART) until he returnsfrom his trip.
Which of the following vaccinations can he safely be given?
explanation:
All of the above are live vaccines, except tetanus, and are therefore contraindicated in an HIV patient not on HAART.
Tetanus vaccine is still important to consider prior to travelling in case of accidental injury.

stem:
A 65-year-old man has extensive oesophageal candidiasis. He is known to be HIV positive.
What treatment, if any, is required?
explanation:
Although oropharyngeal candidiasis may be treated with topical antifungal agents (such as nystatin, clotrimazole, and amphotericinB oral suspension/lozenges) Candida oesophagitis requires oral or IV therapy (usually with ﬂuconazole or itraconazole for at least14-21 days).
Topical therapy is inadequate.

stem:
A 26-year-old homosexual man presented to hospital with a fever, dry cough and dyspnoea. Oropharyngeal candidiasis was noted. He wasfound to be HIV antibody positive and Pneumocystis jirovecii was found on bronchoalveolar lavage. His Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia(PCP) was treated with intravenous co-trimoxazole and he was subsequently started on highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART).
Four weeks later he presented to clinic complaining of weakness and generalised aching. He was taking highly active antiretroviral therapy(zidovudine (AZT), lamivudine (3TC), nelﬁnavir), co-trimoxazole as Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis and ﬂuconazole.
Investigations:
Serum creatine kinase6700 IU/L(24-195)
Myoglobin found in urine.
What is the cause of this problem?
explanation:
Side-effects of zidovudine (AZT) include:bone marrow suppressionmacrocytosis (can be used as a parameter to monitor adherence to therapy)myalgia, andmyopathy.
Lactic acidosis and lipodystrophy are thought to be side-effect common to all nucleoside analogues.
In this case the CK is elevated as the patient is going into a picture of rhabdomyolysis, a known assocation with AZT treatment.

He has just been admitted with new onset congestive cardiac failure. He works in a ﬁsh farm and has no relevant past medical history. Hegives a history of feeling unwell for the last one to two weeks with headaches and muscle aches and pains.
On examination the patient looks relatively well but has a tinge of jaundice and suffusion of the conjunctivae. He has pitting oedema till mid-shin and ﬁne crackles at the lung bases. Pulse is 90 bpm regular and he is afebrile.

A 32-year-old man was referred to clinic with a ten year history of recurrent chest infections. He was diagnosed with common variableimmunodeﬁciency.
Laboratory investigations showed:
IgG6.5 g/L(6.0-13.0)
IgA0.8 g/L(0.8-3.0)

Which of the following options would best prevent recurrent chest infections?
options: Intermittent courses of antibiotics when the patient feels he is developing a chest infection
explanation:
Common variable immunodeﬁciency (CVID) is the most prevalent of the primary immunodeﬁciency diseases. The basic defect inCVID is a failure of B lymphocyte differentiation into plasma cells that produce the various immunoglobulin (Ig) subtypes.
Patients with CVID often have marked reduction in serum levels of both IgG and IgA; approximately 50% of these patients also havereduced IgM. However, some patients have normal IgG levels but functional antibody deﬁciency may be present despite normal IgGsubclass levels.
The diagnosis is based on exclusion of known causes of defects of the humoral immune system. Most cases are sporadic, althoughfamilial cases exist that have various inheritance modes (including autosomal dominant with variable penetrance, autosomalrecessive, and X linked).

His past medical history includes gastritis - for which he takes omeprazole - asthma, and type 2 diabetes mellitus.
He had no recent history of foreign travel but had just returned from a two week holiday to the seaside. Prior to the holiday, he had receiveda short course of clindamycin from his GP for cellulitis.
On examination his abdomen was diffusely tender. He was admitted from clinic for further tests.
Haemoglobin109 g/L(135-180)
Platelets 250 ×10/L (150-400)

C reactive protein178 mg/L(0-10)

Which of the following statements is true regarding this patient's diagnosis and management?
options: Endoscopy has no role in the diagnostic process
Toxin detection from stool is the most widely used diagnostic tool
ELISA-based tests are the most sensitive diagnostic tool in the ﬁrst instance
The patient should be admitted and treated with IV cefuroxime and metronidazole

stem:
This 52-year-old female presents with a one day history of fever and this facial appearance.
The patient is penicillin allergic having had a problems with facial swelling previously.
Which of the following antibiotics would be the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
explanation:
Erysipelas is a Streptococcus pyogenes infection of the deep dermis and subcutis.
Treatment relies upon IV antibiotics such as benzylpenicillin and erythromycin. In a penicillin allergic patient a macrolide is the drugof choice from the above list.

stem:
A 35-year-old gentleman diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia underwent a matched sibling allogeneic haemopoietic stem celltransplant.
One month after the transplant the patient developed profuse haemoptysis, which persists despite platelet support. He also developed lowgrade pyrexia.
You would proceed to do which of the following?
options: Investigate with imaging of the chest
Start empirical treatment with liposomal amphotericin B
Investigate with serological evidence of fungal infection - galactomannan or D-glucan testing and/or PCR for fungal DNA
Proceed to do a bronchoscopy and obtain BAL for further investigation
explanation:
This question covers the use of antifungals in haematology patients.
In patients who are prone to invasive fungal infections it is no longer suggested that empirical therapy with systemic antifungals iscommenced (according to the latest British Committee for Standards in Haematology guidelines).
Serological and/or imaging/biopsy should be sought prior to instituting antifungal therapy, but imaging would be the least invasiveand most easily available modality of choice in order to investigate a suspected fungal infection.

stem:
A 17-year-old girl with sickle cell disease presents with pain in her left thigh.
A plain x ray ﬁlm shows changes consistent with osteomyelitis of the left femur.
Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
Patients with sickle cell disease have a predisposition to develop osteomyelitis due to Salmonella species.
Functional hyposplenism in sickle cell disease also renders sufferers susceptible to infection with encapsulated bacteria(pneumococci, meningococci).

A 72-year-old man presents to the tuberculosis clinic. He has a 6-month history of lower back pain that has been gradually getting worse. Hehas tried taking analgesia, but this is now no longer helping the pain and he is becoming less able to mobilise.
He lives wife his wife on their farm. He has been fully independent until his recent deterioration in mobility.Past medical history includes hypertension, diet-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus and benign prostatic hypertrophy. He reports that he had tuberculosis when he was 24, but this was treated. He can't remember what he was treated with.
An MRI spine shows an L4/5 discitis and a biopsy of this tissue is arranged. Acid-fast bacilli are grown on culture of the biopsy.
What treatment regime should be started?
options: 3 months of Isoniazid, Rifampicin, Pyrazinamide and Ethambutol with a further 6 months of Isoniazid and Rifampicin
6 months of Isoniazid, Rifampicin, Pyrazinamide and Ethambutol with a further 6 months of Isoniazid and Rifampicin
6 months of Isoniazid, Rifampicin, Pyrazinamide and Ethambutol
2 months of Isoniazid, Rifampicin, Pyrazinamide and Ethambutol with a further 7 months of Isoniazid and Rifampicin
2 months of Isoniazid, Rifampicin, Pyrazinamide and Ethambutol with a further 4 months of Isoniazid and Rifampicin
explanation:
Treatment for bone and joint tuberculosis is recommended to continue for two months with the initial phase consisting ofquadruple therapy and the remaining four months as dual therapy. It is recommended not to extend treatment for residualcomplications such as collapsed discs or bending of the spine.
References:
NICE: Tuberculosis

A 42-year-old Zimbabwean man was admitted to the emergency department after becoming unconscious at Heathrow airport shortly afterhis arrival in the United Kingdom.
His wife said that he had been unwell for several weeks, but had complained of a high fever associated with neck stiffness for the past 24hours. Microscopy of his CSF is pictured.
What organism is shown?
explanation:
Diagnosis is by demonstration of C. neoformans in the cerebrospinal ﬂuid, shown on an India ink stain: the thick polysaccharidecapsule is highlighted around the cell (shown in slide).
Cryptococcal meningitis is an AIDS-deﬁning illness occurring when CD4 less than 50 cells/mm and may be associated with apneumonitis.
Cryptococcus can also cause papular skin lesions that resemble molluscum contagiosum.

A 45-year-old type 2 diabetic male presents with a one-day history of swelling of his big toe and foot which is getting worse. He states it isvery hot and swollen and exquisitely painful to touch. He also states that he has been unwell with a fever for the last two hours and hasreduced appetite. He has a past medical history of chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage 2.
On examination, there is erythema of the big toe and half of the medial aspect of the foot which is painful to touch, hot, and swollen. There isstill active movement of all joints and no skin breaks can be seen.
His bloods show a neutrophilia with a C-Reactive Protein of 200 and White Blood Count of 12.4.
He has a temperature of 38.4°C and is tachycardic at 120BPM.
Given the probable diagnosis, what is the recommended initial treatment?
explanation:
This patient is suffering from cellulitis given the history and risk factors described. He is  also exhibiting signs of septic shock and themost effective treatment, in this case, would be to initiate intravenous antibiotic therapy.
Oral ﬂucloxacillin is a reasonable option but in the initial sepsis period, it would be wiser to initiate IV treatment. Colchicine andibuprofen are both used in the treatment of acute gout attacks whereas joint aspiration is reserved for the diagnosis of gout,pseudogout or septic arthritis.
Further reading:
NHS Choices: CellulitisMARKED

He describes the stools as being yellow, frothy and offensive smelling. He has lost 5 kg in weight but is afebrile.
Stool microscopy is shown below.
What is the cause of his diarrhoea?
explanation:
The history is typical of giardiasis: abdominal cramps, bloating and ﬂatulence accompanied by yellow, frothy, greasy and offensive-smelling diarrhoea (steatorrhoea). Fever and vomiting are less usual. Diarrhoea may be chronic if undiagnosed and can lead to smallbowel malabsorption.
The wet mount slide shows cysts of Giardia intestinalis. At higher magniﬁcation you would be able to see the characteristic doublenuceli in each cyst.

explanation:
The CT scan shows a Chagas mega-esophagus with food residue as well as radio-opaque material in the grossly dilated oesophagus.

A 67-year-old man presented to hospital with fever, loin pain and dysuria. These symptoms had been present for three days. There was nopast history of urinary tract infections and he denied any recent history of urinary hesitancy, poor ﬂow or dribbling.
On examination his blood pressure was 85/50 mmHg with a heart rate of 115 beats per minute and temperature 38.9°C. He was slightlysweaty and clammy.
His heart sounds were normal with no added sounds or murmurs and his chest was clear on auscultation. Abdominal examination revealedmild guarding in the right ﬂank. The ECG showed a sinus tachycardia. The chest radiograph was normal. He remained hypotensive and wastransferred to the intensive care unit where a right heart catheter was inserted.
His right heart pressures are shown below:
Right atrial pressure3/2 mmHg
Right ventricle 20/10 mmHg
Pulmonary artery pressure25 mmHg
Pulmonary wedge pressure4 mmHg
What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The answer is a right pyelonephritis; it is important not to be misled by a table of right heart pressures.
The expectation is that since cardiac catheter data are presented that there must be a problem with the heart; however this case isused to illustrate a patient with septic shock as systemic, right atrial and right ventricle  pressures are low.
The clinical history is suggestive of a pyelonephritis particularly as the chest x ray is normal which is likely to exclude a pneumonia.
Behçet's can present with colonic perforation but is unlikely.

He was transferred to the intensive care unit where he underwent tracheal intubation and ventilation. Five days after admission hedeveloped haemoptysis and on examination was found to have coarse crackles in the right lower lung.
A sample from tracheal aspirates was sent to the microbiology laboratory.
The results are as shown.
White blood cell9,000

Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
explanation:
Haemophilus inﬂuenzae is a common causative agent for ventilator-associated pneumonia. It is a Gram negative bacillus. It is foundin increased frequency in smokers and patients with COPD. Infection tends to occur within ﬁve days of hospital admission.
Streptococcus pneumoniae is a Gram positive diplococcus.
Staphylococcus aureus is a Gram positive coccus.
Mycoplasma hominis causes infections of the genitourinary tract.

She complained of regular spiking fevers and rigors and of lethargy and malaise. Physical examination was unremarkable apart from atemperature of 40°C. A peripheral blood ﬁlm is shown below.

You are asked to review a patient with acute respiratory failure due to H1N1 inﬂuenza virus infection. The agreed treatment plan includesusing non-invasive ventilation (NIV).
Which one of the following statements is the most important in relation to NIV?
options: NIV should be started after the mask is secured to the face
A single hose NIV machine is preferable
Personal protective equipment is not required during NIV treatment
Water humidiﬁcation should always be used
A helmet NIV system should not be used
explanation:
Whilst there is no evidence that NIV prevents invasive ventilation in H1N1 patients, it is commonly used as bridging therapy. It isimportant to remember that these are open circuits and still require personal protection for staff.
Ensuring that a well ﬁtting mask is in place before airﬂow starts can reduce the amount of aerosol production. Similarly, avoidingwater humidiﬁcation and use of a closed hood is also advised.
Ideally patients should be nursed in a negative pressure room.
Experience with helmet devices is limited but increasing, and it has been successful in patients who are unable to tolerate the nasalor orofacial devices. The advantage is that it may provide a tighter seal than nasal or orofacial devices. 
Reference:
Anaesthesia UK. Intensive Care Management of Pandemic (H1N1) Inﬂuenza.

A 22-year-old nursery school teacher is referred to clinic by her GP.
She gives several weeks' history of swollen, tender ﬁnger joints. She has no past history of note and has been entirely well apart from a recentviral infection. She had no signiﬁcant travel history. The only sick contacts she could recall were several of the children in her class who hadrecently been off sick with a mild self-limiting illness consisting of a fever, rhinorrhoea and a rash.
On examination the metocarpo-phalangeal joints and proximal interphalangeal joints of both hands are swollen and tender.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Parvovirus B19 is a single-strand DNA virus. The most widely known clinical manifestation of parvovirus B19 is erythema infectiosum('slapped cheek syndrome'), a mild viral illness of childhood characterised by a classic exanthem in which both cheeks appear brightred as though they had been slapped.
Although usually a benign self-limiting viral illness, parvovirus B19 infection may have more serious sequelae. The virus has a tropismfor rapidly dividing erythrocyte precursors which they infect and destroy. Thus, no reticulocytes (immature erythrocytes) areavailable to replace aging or damaged erythrocytes as they are cleared by the reticuloendothelial system. This may not have anysigniﬁcant impact on otherwise healthy individuals, but can trigger an aplastic crisis - particularly in patients withhaemoglobinopathies.
Parvovirus B19 infection may also be associated with a symmetrical post-infectious arthritis, affecting the small joints of the handsand feet. The knees or elbows are rarely involved.
The arthritis is much more common in adults, particularly in women, and may persist for weeks to months (even years in a smallnumber of patients). The arthritis may mimic rheumatoid arthritis. Unlike rheumatoid arthritis, the post-infectious arthritisassociated with parvovirus B19 does not cause permanent damage to bones or joints.
Rheumatoid arthritis is a possibillty but the fact she's been around children with viral illnesses means you should exclude parvovirusﬁrst.

A 19-year-old woman presents with severe left iliac fossa pain of acute onset.
On examination she has a temperature of 38.0°C. Pelvic examination reveals uterine and left adnexal tenderness. Gram stain of the cervicalexudates demonstrates Gram negative intracellular diplococci.
Which of the following statements applies?
options: Serologic tests to detect the presence of antibody in the patient's serum is useful for diagnosis
Infection outside the genital tract in rare.
Treatment is contraindicated in the absence of Gram negative diplococci on Gram staining.
Contact tracing should be initiated following treatment
Disease notiﬁcation to the Health Protection Unit (HPU) is required
explanation:
The patient has pelvic inﬂammatory disease secondary to Neisseria gonorrhoea.
This is the second commonest sexually transmitted infection (STI) in the United Kingdom. It is seen as Gram negative intracellulardiplococcus on Gram staining. The absence of organisms on Gram stain does not exclude infection. Culture is the gold standarddiagnostic tool.
Patients may present with:UrethritisEpididymitisEndocervicitis, orPelvic inﬂammatory disease.
Patients may also be be asymptomatic.
Contact tracing is important for treatment of other infected persons and prevention of re-infection following treatment.
The presence of antibody in the patient's serum could be an indication of prior infection and is not an appropriate diagnostic test.
Disseminated gonococcal infection occurs in approximately 1% of cases and can cause septic arthritis, arthralgia, endocarditis,meningitis, and fevers.
All women with suspected gonococcal infection should undergo a pregnancy test as neonatal intrapartum infection can causeconjunctivitis neonatorum and disseminated infection.

A 32-year-old man with HIV disease presents to clinic eight weeks after starting highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART).
He had been well before starting therapy but now complains of lassitude and weakness. His HAART consists of two nucleoside analogues(zidovudine [AZT] and lamivudine [3TC]) and a protease inhibitor (nelﬁnavir). He also takes co-trimoxazole as prophylaxis againstPneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia.
Test Pre-treatment8 weeks after starting treatmentNormal
Haemoglobin125 g/L 81 g/L (130-180)
MCV 96 fL 101 fL (80-96)
What is the most likely cause of his anaemia?
options: Inﬁltration of bone marrow by Mycobacterium avium intracellulare
explanation:
Antiretroviral therapies are frequent causes of anaemia in HIV-seropositive patients.
Of these, zidovudine (AZT) is the agent that most frequently causes anaemia, usually by bone marrow suppression and patients canbecome transfusion-dependent in severe cases.
Other side-effects of zidovudine include:MyalgiaMyopathyMyositisPancytopenia, andLactic acidosis.
Blue discolouration of the nails is a rare side-effect.

stem:
A 39-year-old Ghanaian man presents to the Emergency department following his ﬁrst grand-mal seizure.
He has recently returned from a three-month holiday in Ghana where he was diagnosed with an ischaemic stroke after he developed rightsided weakness. He gives a further history of low grade fevers and a dry cough on and off over several months.
On examination his GCS is 15/15. His blood pressure is 110/65 mmHg. Neurological examination revealed a mild right hemiparesis. Therewas no meningism or papilloedema.
He undergoes a magnetic resonance scan of the brain that demonstrates several ring enhancing lesions.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
From the history given, it is likely that this patient has toxoplasmosis, a central nervous system disease most commonly seen in HIV.
The history of low grade fevers and a generalised malaise for months, as well as a clinical suspicion of toxoplasmosis should promptan HIV antibody test.
The ﬁndings of several ring enhancing lesions on MRI combined with low grade pyrexia, focal neurological deﬁcit and seizures ismost suggestive of toxoplasmosis. Toxoplasmosis usually occurs in the presence of a CD4 count <200/mm.
Progressive multifocal leucoencephalopathy is caused by the JC virus and usually occurs in the presence of CD4 count <100/mm.
MRI shows multifocal lesions in the subcortical white matter.
Primary CNS lymphoma should be suspected if the patient has no response to anti-toxoplasma therapy. It usually presents withaltered mental status.
CNS tuberculosis most commonly occurs when the CD4 count is <100/mm. It presents with headache, fever, meningism, andimpaired conscious level. Brain imaging shows meningeal enhancement and occasionally, tuberculomas. Diagnosis is by CSF culturefor Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

stem:
A 45-year-old HIV-seropositive man attended the outpatient clinic for the results of a fasting serum lipid test. He had been diagnosed withHIV disease two years previously when he presented with Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP). His CD4 T cell count at diagnosis was 50cells/mm (800-1200) and an HIV viral load measured by quantitative PCR of 1.2 ×10 copies per ml.
After treatment for the PCP had been completed he was started on highly active antiretroviral therapy. Two years after commencing onantiretrovirals, his CD4 count had risen to 350 cells/mm with an undetectable viral load.
Baseline resistance testing prior to starting antiretroviral had shown high-level resistance to non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors.His current medications consisted of zidovudine, lamivudine, lopinavir and ritonavir.
His serum lipids were normal before starting antiretroviral therapy. During serial measurements over the preceding twelve months, hisserum lipid proﬁles had been noted to be abnormal. He had been reviewed by the clinic dietician who had suggested amendments to hisdiet.
The most recent fasting lipid sample (taken two weeks previously) had shown:
Serum cholesterol4.1 mmol/L(<5.2)
Serum triglyceride10.2 mmol/L(0.5-1.7)
Which of the following treatment options would be most appropriate to treat his dyslipidaemia?
explanation:
Lipodystrophy, lipoatrophy and alterations in serum lipid values have been observed in patients with human immunodeﬁciency virus(HIV) disease taking highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). Elevated serum lipid levels have been associated with prematurecoronary artery disease.
Hypertriglyceridaemia is also thought to contribute to central fat deposition and insulin resistance that is also seen in these patients.

A 37-year-old intravenous drug user, not receiving any medication, presents with fever, dyspnoea, night sweats, weight loss and non-productive cough of several weeks in duration.
He has dry rales on physical examination, and chest radiography reveals diffuse interstitial inﬁltrates. On further investigation, he is found tobe HIV-positive, and the CD4 cell count is 95 cells/mm. Induced sputum is negative for Pneumocystis carnii.
Which of these investigations would you do to conﬁrm the diagnosis?
explanation:
The sensitivity after using induced sputum is about 70% but bronchoalveolar lavage increases that sensitivity to about 94%. If thebronchoalveolar lavage is still negative then a transbronchial biopsy should be done mainly to look for other diagnoses.
Pulmonary function test especially low diffusing capacity of the lung for carbon monoxide (DCO) can support the diagnosis of
Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia but cannot conﬁrm the diagnosis because other diseases can also cause a low DCO.
Gallium scan increased uptake also only supports the diagnosis but cannot be used for diagnosis.
Transbronchial biopsy is invasive despite having a high sensitivity. It should be done after inducing sputum and bronchoalveolarlavage has been done.
Open lung biopsy is quite invasive despite having sensitivities and speciﬁcities of up to 100%. It should be done after inducingsputum and bronchoalveolar lavage has been done.

You are asked to review a patient with acute respiratory failure due to H1N1 inﬂuenza virus infection.
She is intubated and ventilated. She has large volumes of gastric ﬂuid aspirated from her nasogastric tube. She currently only has peripheralintravenous access.
Which of the following treatment options is most appropriate?
options: Oseltamivir 150 mg orally bd for 10 days
Oseltamivir 75 mg orally bd for 10 days
Oseltamivir 150 mg orally bd for 5 days
explanation:
For critically ill patients with conﬁrmed or suspected H1N1, oseltamivir 150 mg bd for ten days is the recommended treatment.
However, in this case, the large volumes of gastric aspirate suggest that enteral absorption may not be effective. The only parenteralalternative is zanamivir.
This can be safely given using peripheral venous access.
For hospitalized inﬂuenza patients with suspected or known gastric statis, gastric malabsorption, gastrointestinal bleeding, or forpatients suspected or conﬁrmed with oseltamivir-resistant inﬂuenza virus infection, intravenous zanamivir should be considered.
There are currently two ways to obtain IV zanamivir: enrollment in a clinical trial through a clinical site, or through a compassionateuse request through GlaxoSmithKline with FDA approval.
Reference:
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Antiviral Agents for Inﬂuenza.

A 46-year-old man presents with jaundice.
A liver screen demonstrates negative HBs antigen and anti-HBs antibody.
What additional test would help conﬁrm that his hepatitis was due to hepatitis B virus?
explanation:
Hepatitis B core antigen is an intracellular antigen that is present in infected cells.Anti-HBc antibody is present throughout infection.Anti-HBc of the IgM class is present in acute infection and persists in the period between the disappearance of HBsAg and theappearance of anti-HBs.Anti-HBc of the IgG class is present along with anti-HBs in patients recovering from acute infection, and with HBsAg in thosewith chronic infection.
The presence of isolated anti-HBc signiﬁes one of three possibilities:1. The patient is in the period of acute hepatitis B between the disappearance of the HBsAg and the appearance of anti-HBs2. Anti-HBs has fallen to undetectable levels following recovery from acute hepatitis B3. Chronic HBV infection where the HBsAg titre has fallen to undetectable levels.
HBe antigen is a marker of replication and infectivity.
HBe Ag to anti-HBe antibody seroconversion usually occurs early in acute infection; however it is occasionally delayed for manyyears in patients with chronic hepatitis B infection.
The ALT may be normal in an inactive carrier state.

A 43-year-old HIV-positive man presented with this rash.
He had been treated for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) six months previously when he presented for the ﬁrst time. His currentmedication included highly active antiretrovial therapy (zidovudine [AZT], lamivudine [3TC] and nevirapine) and co-trimoxazole as PCPprophylaxis. His CD4 count was 210 cells/mm with an undetectable HIV viral load.
What is the cause of his rash?
explanation:
The slide shows the typical rash of herpes zoster (shingles), caused by VZV.
HIV-positive patients are more prone to herpes zoster regardless of their CD4 count.
In addition to the typical dermatomal distribution of the vesicular rash, HIV patients occasionally have vesicles scattered in adjacentdermatomes.

A diplomat with the Commonwealth is going to Uganda to observe the elections. He has had his vaccinations in preparation for the trip.
He has previously been treated for schizophrenia but he is now better and is able to work.
He is worried about malaria and you advise him about protecting himself from mosquito bites. He wants to know the best medication forprophylaxis against malaria.
Which of these drugs would you recommend?
explanation:
Doxycycline prophylaxis is the safest option with less resistance in many parts of the world compared to the other options available.
Chloroquine prophylaxis is wrong because of high levels of resistance to the drug around the world.
Meﬂoquine prophylaxis could be used but this patient has a mental illness which is a contradiction for its use.
Proguanil prophylaxis is wrong but it can be used in combination with atovaquone for prophylaxis. Proguanil should not be usedalone as malaria could develop resistance to it. Atovaquone and proguanil are used for prophylaxis especially where there are highlevels of resistance against most of the other drugs.
Sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine prophylaxis cannot be used because of the high levels of resistance against the drug.

stem:
A 34-year-old woman attended the genitourinary medicine clinic complaining of a vaginal discharge.
She had seen her GP about it a week ago, who had prescribed her some clotrimazole pessaries following which she had no relief. She deniedany itching, but described it as malodorous especially following intercourse.
On examination there was a thin white vaginal discharge with a pH of 5.9. Microscopy demonstrated Lactobacilli with Gram variable rods.
Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for seven days
Erythromycin 500 mg two times a day for seven days
explanation:
This patient describes bacterial vaginosis, a common diagnosis in women of childbearing age.
Patients will often describe a malodorous "ﬁshy" thin, milky white discharge which is not itchy. The ﬁshy odour can be elicited byadding 10% potassium hydroxide to the vaginal discharge. The vaginal pH is usually greater than 4.5.
Risk factors for bacterial vaginosis include the intrauterine coil device, vaginal douching and number of sexual partners.
Bacterial vaginosis has been implicated in the development of pelvic inﬂammatory diseases. Patients may be asymptomatic. Whereidentiﬁed it should be treated in patients who are symptomatic or pregnant. The ﬁrst line treatment of bacterial vaginosis in the UK ismetronidazole 400 mg twice daily given for seven days. Alternatively, a single dose of oral metronidazole 2 g may be given especiallyif patient adherence is an issue.
Azithromycin is used in the treatment of Chlamydia, and ceftriaxone in the treatment of gonorrhoea.
In the US, CDC have updated treatment recommendations for bacterial vaginosis (2010). Metronidazole 500 mg orally twice a dayfor seven days is the recomended therapy and alternatives include several tinidazole regimens or clindamycin (oral or intravaginal).
Additional regimens include metronidazole (750 mg extended release tablets once daily for seven days), or a single dose ofclindamycin intravaginal cream, although data on the performance of these alternative regimens are limited.

A 29-year-old IV drug user presents with a two week history of non-productive cough, fatigue, shortness of breath and fever. On examination,he has a respiratory rate of 28, a heart rate of 90 and was hypoxic on exercise.
His blood test results were as follows:
Haemoglobin110 g/L(135-180)
White cell count3 ×10/L (4-11)
Neutrophils2.5 ×10/L (1.5-7.4)
