Chest x rayNormal
Which of the following investigations would be diagnostic?
explanation:
This patient has Pneumocystis jiroveci, formerly known as Pneumocystis carinii.
P. jiroveci, formerly thought to be a protozoan, is an atypical fungus that is not susceptible to antifungals. Transmission is airborne,usually in childhood, with reactivation in immunosuppressive states.

A 22-year-old lady, with lupus and antiphospholipid syndrome presented to the Rheumatology clinic with sharp chest pain across her rightside. This pain had started three days prior to presentation.
She had some shortness of breath and reported that she has a vesicular rash that had started one day ago over that area.
She weighs 65 kg and her medications are:
Methotrexat20 mg once weekly
Prednisolone30 mg once a day
Aspirin 75 mg once a day
Folic Acid5 mg once a day
She was admitted to rheumatology and underwent a CTPA which showed no pulmonary emboli, but widespread bilateral changes of subsolidnodules and ground-glass opaciﬁcation.
Her shortness of breath started to get worse and her observations were taken: temperature 39.1 °C, blood pressure 107/55, heart rate 122,oxygen saturation 88% on air.
What is the best treatment for her likely diagnosis?
options: Treat with aciclovir 650 mg intravenous 8 hourly
Treat with 1 g intravenous amoxicillin 8 hourly
Treat with 1 g intravenous amoxicillin 8 hourly and 500 mg oral clarythromycin 12 hourly
Treat with 800 mg aciclovir orally 5 times daily
explanation:
The most likely diagnosis for this immunocompromised lady with sharp pain and a vesicular rash is varicella-zoster chickenpox. Sheis systemically unwell with it and has widespread pulmonary changes that are consistent with varicella pneumonitis.
The treatment of choice in an immunocompromised host with varicella-zoster is intravenous aciclovir at a dose of 10 mg/Kg.
References:

A 65-year-old female was referred to your practice with a history of having vesicles which later turned into scabs around the inner thighfollowing the L dermatome.
She is said to have had a burning-like sensation following the same dermatome prior to the development of the vesicles. The vesicles areonly on the left side of her body.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Herpes zoster usually has a prodrome pain before the vesicles appear. It usually follows a particular dermatome but in immunesuppression the disease may affect more than one dermatome.
Herpes simplex II is the wrong answer. Herpes simplex II vesicles may appear but they never follow a particular dermatome.
Tinea inguinalis is the wrong answer. Tinea inguinalis never forms vesicles but there is the presence of scabs around the groin or anyother fold.
Streptococcal scalded skin syndrome is the wrong answer. This appears like a burn. It appears as bullae which eventually burst. Itcould be generalised.
Staphylococcus aureus skin infection is the wrong answer. It could sometimes appear as streptococcal scalded skin syndrome, butthere are more likely to be pustules.

A 24-year-old Irishman presented with a ten week history of progressively worsening exertional dyspnoea and a dry cough. He was otherwisewell in himself.
Auscultation of his chest revealed ﬁne inspiratory crackles to the mid-zones. He was afebrile.
His chest radiograph is shown below. A Heaf test was negative.
Which of the following investigations will be most helpful in establishing a diagnosis?
explanation:
The chest x ray shows bilateral reticulonodular shadowing and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. The most likely diagnosis issarcoidosis.
Most cases of sarcoid present between 20 and 40 years of age with a slightly increased incidence in women.

stem:
A 21-year-old man presents with a two week history of increasing right knee pain and swelling. He has also noticed pain at his heels whichmakes walking uncomfortable. He also describes irritation of both his eyes.
He has no genital symptoms. He has had unprotected insertive anal and oral sex with six casual male sexual partners in the last year. His lastsexual contact was three weeks ago.
He has no signiﬁcant past medical history and is not taking any medication. His brother has ankylosing spondylitis.
Examination reveals tenderness of the right knee joint with reduced range of movement. A patellar tap is present. His right conjunctiva isinjected but pupil and visual acuity are normal. Medial anterior border of calcaneum is tender bilaterally. He has no skin lesions.
Knee joint aspiration is carried out and reveals 60000 leucocytes/uL. No organisms are seen.
What test is most likely to show the cause of his symptoms?
explanation:
This man has sexually acquired reactive arthritis (SARA).
This is probably an immune mediated phenomenon linked to the immune response to uro-genital micro-organisms. It affects menmore than women (10:1) and the HLA B27 gene increases susceptibility by up to 50 times. Typically it affects one to six jointsasymmetrically in lower limbs, especially feet, ankles and knees.
It may be associated with conjunctivitis, iritis, circinate balanitis, tenosynovitis or enthesitis (especially affecting Achilles tendon andplantar fascia attachment to calcaneum as in this case). Rarely cardiac lesions including tachycardia, LV dilatation, pericarditis oraortic valve disease can occur.
Renal lesions including proteinuria, haematuria and sterile pyuria can occur in up to 50% but are usually asymptomatic.
The most common causative organism is Chlamydia trachomatis, though Neisseria gonorrhoeae has also been shown to causeSARA and Ureaplasma urealyticum may also be linked.

A 36-year-old gay man presented to hospital with a four week history of progressively worsening dyspnoea, dry cough and fever.
His chest x ray showed bilateral diffuse airspace shadowing and Pneumocystis jirovecii was isolated from bronchial washings followingbronchoscopy. His CD4 T-lymphocyte count was 88 cells/mm.
He had a history of rash with co-trimoxazole and was started on treatment for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia with trimethoprim anddapsone.
His condition improved within twenty four hours, but ﬁve days later he became increasingly breathless again and was cyanosed. His oxygensaturations were measured at 85% by pulse oxymetry and his PaO was 12.1 kPa (11.3-12.6).
What is the most appropriate immediate course of action?
explanation:
The patient has methaemoglobinaemia caused by dapsone. Drugs that cause methaemoglobinaemia include:PhenacetinSulphonamidesDapsonePrimaquineLidocaineProcaineBenzocaine.
In methaemoglobinaemia, an abnormally large proportion of the iron in haem is oxidised to the ferric state leading to impairedoxygen transport and anaemic hypoxia. Patients appear to be cyanosed, though the cyanosis does not clear when oxygen isadministered.
Clinical features of methaemoglobinaemia depend on the MetHb levels in blood. The discolouration of blood and appearance ofcyanosis manifests when the MetHb levels reach 15-20%.
Levels between 20-45% are associated with dyspnoea, lethargy, dizziness and headaches.

You are working in a medical admissions unit.
Following the British HIV Association guidelines which of the following conditions should prompt you to consider performing an HIV test?
explanation:
In 2012 it was estimated that 21% of people living with HIV in the UK are undiagnosed. The BHIVA 2008 guidelines recommend thatin low prevalence areas (where HIV prevalence is less than 2 per 1000) then HIV tests should be performed for a wide range of'clinical indicator' diseases, amongst which are the options listed here. A full list can be found in the guidelines referenced below.
It is in the capability of every doctor, nurse and health care professional to perform an HIV test. HIV is a treatable condition with anormal life expectancy if diagnosed early, and therefore no longer requires pre-test counselling. The patient should be informed ofthe beneﬁts of testing and how and when the result will be provided to them as with any other medical test.
If HIV is detected early it dramatically reduces the morbidity and mortality associated with HIV. Furthermore from a public healthaspect it is thought that 50% of new infections occur in people unaware that they have HIV.
Reference:
British HIV Association (BHIVA). UK National Guidelines for HIV Testing 2008.

A 22-year-old student presents with a two week history of vulval itching, dyspareunia, and a greenish malodorous vaginal discharge. She hasa history of type 1 diabetes mellitus. She has had unprotected sexual intercourse several times over the last few weeks.
On examination her cervix is erythematous with petechial lesions. The pH of the discharge is 7.0. Genital wet prep shows a high number ofwhite blood cells and a protozoan organism.
Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
Trichomonas vaginalis causes:ItchingBurningDyspareunia, andDysuria.
It is an anaerobic protozoan which thrives in more alkaline conditions. The pH of the discharge is greater than 6.5.
T. vaginalis does not have a cyst form and therefore is transmitted directly, for example, through sexual transmission. It causesinﬂammation of the vaginal endometrium and therefore makes it more susceptible to other sexually transmitted infections.
Treatment of T. vaginalis is with metronidazole. Sexual partners should also be treated, as they may be asymptomatic carriers.

explanation:

A 15-year-old girl presented to the Emergency department with diﬃculty breathing.
She was a known asthmatic who had seen her general practitioner the previous day with a sore throat. He had diagnosed tonsillitis and hadprescribed a 5 day course of oral amoxicillin. The patient had been diagnosed with ulcerative colitis three years previously. Her regularmedication included inhaled salbutamol and beclomethasone and mesalazine 400 mg tds.
On examination she was alert and oriented but was in considerable distress with laboured breathing. Inspiratory wheeze was noted. She waspale, sweaty and cyanosed. Her temperature was 36.5°C, pulse 120/minute and regular, blood pressure 90/35 mmHg. The lungs were clearand the remainder of the examination was normal.
She was given high-ﬂow oxygen through a face mask but despite this her breathing became increasingly diﬃcult.
What is the most likely pathogen?
explanation:
The most likely diagnosis is acute epiglottitis.
Sudden airway obstruction may occur and it is vital to obtain the assistance of an anaesthetist urgently. No attempt should be madeto visualise the epiglottis until an anaesthetist is present as there is a high risk of causing acute airway obstruction by touching theinﬂamed tissue.
The diagnosis may be conﬁrmed on direct visualisation of a cherry-red epiglottis.
Early intubation is essential, especially in cases where there is respiratory distress. Adult epiglottitis is much less common but has ahigher mortality.
The usual causative organism is Haemophilus inﬂuenzae type b.

A 42-year-old businessman presented to the Emergency department six weeks after returning from a business trip to Thailand.
On examination he was febrile (38.5°C) and had generalised lymphadenopathy and a diffuse macular rash. Atypical lymphocytes were seenon a blood ﬁlm. He had taken meﬂoquine as malaria prophylaxis.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Acute HIV disease (seroconversion illness) occurs two to 12 weeks following exposure to HIV and is said to occur in 40-80% ofindividuals.
The typical presentation is with:FeverSevere pharyngitisGeneralised lymphadenopathy, andA macular or maculo-papular rash.
The presentation may mimic glandular fever, though the pharyngitis associated with acute HIV is usually more severe and a rashonly occurs in glandular fever when ampicillin has been given.
Dengue fever has an incubation of 21 days.
Atypical lymphocytes, also known as reactive lymphocytes are usually seen with viral infections.Atypical lymphocytes are mostcommonly seen in patients who have infectious mononucleosis. They are also caused by drug reactions (phenytoin), stress, viral orbacterial infections, allergies, autoimmune diseases, thyroid problems and malignancy.In most cases, atypical lymphocytes stemfrom a particular cause, such as a sore throat or a recent vaccination.

On examination he was fully conscious with a Glasgow coma scale score of 15/15. He was febrile (38°C) with pulse 80 beats per minute insinus rhythm and blood pressure 130/75 mmHg. There was no nuchal rigidity. Neurological examination revealed an expressive dysphasiaand mild right sided weakness.

A 36-year-old woman presents with multiple painful lesions on her labia and upper thigh. She ﬁrst noticed these three days prior topresentation. She has no signiﬁcant past medical history and had a negative HIV test one month ago. She had unprotected sexualintercourse two weeks ago whilst on holiday in Rwanda.
On examination she has multiple erythematous pustules on her labia and upper thighs, two of the pustules appear ulcerated. She also haspainful inguinal lymphadenopathy.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The most likely diagnosis is chancroid.
It is caused by Haemophilus ducreyi, a Gram negative rod which is frequent cause of genital ulceration in Rwanda.
The incubation period is approximately one week, following which erythematous papules develop on the external genitalia andsurrounding regions. These later develop into pustules and may erode into sloughy haemorrhagic ulcers.
Painful lymphadenopathy is common. Lymphadenopathy may also be seen in lymphogranuloma venereum and granulomainguinale, however LGV initially presents as a single painless ulcer with secondary infection occurring two to six weeks later.
Granuloma inguinale is caused by Klebsiella granulomatosis. Also known as donovaniasis, it causes indolent painless ulcers. Regionallymphadenopathy is rare. The incubation period is one to three months.
Whilst HSV is one of the most common causes of genital ulceration in the world, it is surpassed by chancroid in Rwanda. Tenderlymphadenopathy in HSV may be accompanied by systemic symptoms such as fever and headache.

A 10-year-old boy is noticed to be jaundiced on return from a holiday in Africa with his parents. He is on antimalarial prophylaxis.
His complete blood count shows haemoglobin of 80 g/L, with Heinz bodies and blister cells on blood ﬁlm examination.
Which of the following relates to this disorder?
options: Transfusion is strictly merited in each case
The antimalarial prophylaxis has no relation to the laboratory ﬁndings
It is most commonly precipitated by peas
Treatment involves strict avoidance of known precipitants
This is a common autosomal dominant disorder
explanation:
This question relates to the management of G-6-PD deﬁciency.
G-6-PD is the most common inherited enzyme defect in humans; an X linked inheritance pattern.
It is mostly commonly precipitated by several classes of drugs, including antimalarials and is also associated with ingestion of broadbeans (favism).
Treatment revolves around avoidance of all known precipitating factors, and blood product support should only be given in unstable,symptomatic patients.

A 30-year-old intravenous drug user has been complaining of back pain for the last six months. Two months ago he developed a backdeformity with malaise; he also claims his clothes no longer ﬁt him.
On examination he is slightly wasted and afebrile. He has a kyphosis in the thoracic area.
Laboratory values show
White blood cell (WBC)9100 cells/mm4000-11000 mm
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)40 mm/hr20 mm/hr
The radiograph shows well maintained disc spaces with erosion of the T vertebral body and fusiform swelling from T-T.
What is the mostly likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Tuberculosis is common in intravenous drug users. The radiographic description is typical of TB of the spine (Pott's disease). Pott'sdisease affects the thoracic spine instead of the lumbar vertebrae which have the greatest blood supply. The other infections of thespine are usually found in the lumbar spine.
Brucella spine (brucellosis of the spine) is the wrong option. The signs and symptoms will be very similar to Pott's disease, but theinfection will often be in the lumbar region and not in the thoracic region.
Fungal osteomyelitis is the wrong option. Like most of the other infections it will affect the lumbar spine.
Kaposi's sarcoma of the spine is the wrong option. It is more likely to affect the vertebral spines and is more likely to affect thelumbar vertebrae.
Staphylococcus aureus spine infection is the wrong option. The infection will show signiﬁcant narrowing of the disc spaces and theinfection will be in the lumbar region.

What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Her symptoms are suggestive of either infectious mononucleosis or acute HIV infection.
Acute Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is less common in adults as it is usually acquired in teenage years and a diffuse macular rash mostoften occurs following administration of ampicillin.
Acute HIV is the most likely answer, particularly in light of her recent travel to sub-Saharan Africa.
Although no details of speciﬁc 'risky' exposure are given, this remains the best answer.

A 38-year-old male who is the brother of the British High Commissioner in Kampala, Uganda went to visit his brother about eight months agofor a two week holiday.
He took meﬂoquine for prophylaxis and he defaulted on the medications.
Now he reports having fevers, chills, rigours and headaches. You suspect malaria and send his blood slides to the laboratory. The thick bloodslide shows parasites that are large with fragmented cytoplasm. The thin ﬁlm shows enlarged red cells containing amoeboid parasites withSchuffner's nodes.
Which of these malarial parasites is likely to be causing the disease?
explanation:
The incubation period of P. vivax can go up to six months or more with malaria being caused by hypnozoites. The malaria episodehappened eight months after returning from Africa. The picture of the thin ﬁlm and thick ﬁlm is diagnostic for P. vivax.
P. falciparum is wrong because its incubation is normally around six days though it can go till 14 days or more. Its thin ﬁlm usuallyshows many ring forms of crescent-shaped gametocytes.
P. knowlesi is wrong because it usually affects apes and monkeys and is usually isolated in the forests around South East Asia.
P. ovale is wrong because it is quite rare. The incubation period is similar to that of P. vivax but on the thick ﬁlm the parasites aremore compact and smaller. On the thin ﬁlm the red blood cells appear oval with ragged ends.
P. malariae is also wrong because it is rare. Its incubation could go up to14 days like P. falciparum. The thick ﬁlm will show a fewcompact rings or small neat schizonts or small round gametocytes with yellow-brown pigment. The thin ﬁlm will show red bloodcells in band forms.

A 24-year-old woman presents with a severe headache of sudden onset and fevers.
On examination she has a temperature of 38°C and nuchal rigidity. On further questioning she reveals that she has been treated for similarsymptoms twice in the past and has been diagnosed with a complement deﬁciency.
Which of the following is most likely to be found on Gram stain of her cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF)?
explanation:
This patient has meningococcal meningitis as suggested by her presenting features and the history of complement deﬁciency.
The causative agent, Neisseria meningitidis, is seen as Gram negative diplococci on Gram staining.
Gram negative bacilli would be suggestive of organisms such as Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, and pseudomonas.
Gram positive cocci in clumps suggest staphlococci, and Gram positive cocci in chains suggest streptococci.
Viral meningitis may present with multiple lymphocytes on Gram stain of CSF but no organisms seen.

A 38-year-old Caucasian man with HIV attended the clinic for review.
He had been diagnosed with HIV infection three years previously after presenting to hospital with disseminated herpes zoster. His CD4 T cellcount at the time of diagnosis was 100 cells/mm (800-1200). He was started on high-dose valaciclovir and subsequently on highly activeantiretroviral therapy consisting of zidovudine, lamivudine and lopinavir.
He was also prescribed co-trimoxazole as prophylaxis against Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and ﬂuconazole for oropharyngealcandidiasis.
Seven months later, his CD4 count had risen to 210 cells/mm and his HIV viral load, measured by quantitative PCR, was undetectable.
As part of his routine panel of blood tests taken at his three monthly review, fasting serum lipid levels showed:
Serum cholesterol8.1 mmol/L(<5.2)
Serum triglyceride4.2 mmol/L(0.45-1.69)
Dietary modiﬁcations were made, with which he remained compliant, but despite this a repeat sample taken two months later showedidentical values.
Which of the following is the best option for treating this patient's dyslipidaemia?
explanation:
Lipodystrophy, lipoatrophy and alterations in serum lipid values have been observed in patients with human immunodeﬁciency virus(HIV) disease taking highly active antiretroviral therapy.
Elevated serum lipid levels have been associated with premature coronary artery disease. The causes of these changes are likely tobe multifactorial, but appear much commoner in patients taking protease inhibitors.

A 44-year-old HIV seropositive patient is seen in a routine outpatient appointment.
He was diagnosed with HIV disease two years ago when he presented with Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) with a CD4 T-lymphocytecount of 40 cells/mm. After being treated for PCP he was started on combination antiretroviral therapy. His initial response to antiretroviraltherapy had been promising, with an increase in his CD4 count (210 cells/mm) and achieving an undetectable HIV viral load in the
peripheral blood.
One year ago, his CD4 count started to fall and HIV RNA became detectable in peripheral blood. An HIV viral resistance test conﬁrmedresistance to all of his antiretroviral drugs. The patient admitted that over the preceding three months that he had only been taking histherapy intermittently. Despite the risks, he decided that he did not wish to have any further antiviral therapy. At this point, his CD4 countwas 20 cells/mm with a very high HIV viral load of 120,000 copies/ml.
Seven months ago he presented with malaise, weight loss (8 kg), fevers and night sweats. Mycobacterium avium intracellulare (MAI) wasisolated from a blood culture and he was started on therapy with ethambutol and rifabutin. He subsequently agreed to re-start antiretroviraltherapy.
During his clinic consultation, he states that he has noticed a steady deterioration in his visual acuity over the past four weeks. His currentmedications include stavudine (d4T), didanosine (ddI), nevirapine, ethambutol, and rifabutin. On examination, fundoscopy is normal.
His last CD4 count, taken one month ago was 30 cells/mm, with an HIV viral load of 2500 copies/ml.
What is the most likely cause of his reduction in visual acuity?
explanation:
Loss of visual acuity in this case is most consistent with ethambutol-induced optic neuritis.
Ethambutol may produce optic neuritis which decreases visual acuity and which appears to be related to dose and duration oftreatment. Symptoms generally start between four months and one year after starting therapy.
The effects are generally reversible when administration of ethambutol is discontinued promptly. In rare cases recovery may bedelayed for one year or more and the effect may possibly be irreversible in these cases.

A 58-year-old man is diagnosed with HIV after presenting to his GP with a case of multi-dermatomal shingles. He was found to have a CD4count of 480 cells/ μ L.
Which of the following statements are true in relation to immunisation for this man?
options: He should be vaccinated against Hepatitis B, pneumococcus, and yearly against inﬂuenza
The Haemophilus inﬂuenzae B vaccine is contraindicated
He should be given DTP and Men C if he missed them in childhood
There is no need to vaccinate him against varicella as he has just had shingles
explanation:
This question assesses knowledge of live versus inactivated vaccines and how immunocompromise effects which vaccines shouldbe administered.
People with HIV are at risk of Hep B, invasive pneumococcal disease and severe morbidity from inﬂuenza. These are all inactivatedvaccines and can be given at any CD4 count. Hepatitis B is given as a course of three injections at double dose and booster asrequired. The pneumococcal vaccine PPV23 is a single dose but could be boosted 5-10 years later. The inﬂuenza vaccine should beadministered yearly.
Men C is only recommended in people under 25. Additionally the oral polio vaccine is not recommended in HIV as it is a live vaccine.However the parenteral polio vaccine is acceptable.
The MMR vaccine is a live vaccine that is contraindicated in patients with a CD4 count of less than 200 cells/ μ L but could be safelyadministered in this patient with his CD4 count of 480 cells/ μ L.
Haemophilus inﬂuenzae B vaccine is an inactivated vaccine that can be given to patients at any CD4 count. Although Haemophilusinﬂuenzae is an issue in people with HIV it is the pneumococcal vaccine that is recommended for all HIV patients. However it is onlyrecommended for those who have splenic dysfunction, recurrent pulmonary infections or for those who have had previousHaemophilus inﬂuenzae disease with risk of recurrence.
The shingles vaccine is thought to be safe and immunogenic even in those who have recently had shingles. However it must beused with caution in any immunocompromised state and should not be used in patients with a CD4 count of less than 200 cells/ μ L.

She has no dysuria or frequency. She reports she has noticed four episodes of haematuriapreviously, but these have always resolved spontaneously after a day or two.
She reports she is usually ﬁt and well apart from hearing aids that she has needed since birth. This doesn't seem unusual to her as both heryounger sister also has needed hearing aids since birth. She works as a primary school teacher and lives with her mother and her sister. Herparents divorced when she was 7 years-old and she has not had any contact with her father since.
On examination, she has an abdomen that is soft and non-tender. Her Rinne test was positive and her Weber test was equally heard in bothears.

A 25-year-old male with newly diagnosed HIV was found to have a CD4 count of 53 cells/ μ L. He was tested for Hepatitis B. His serologyresults were as follows:
Hep B eAgnegative
Hep B eAbpositive
Hep B sAgpositive
Which of the following statements is true?
options: He should be immunised against Hepatitis B with a double strength vaccination
He should be placed on an antiretroviral regime that is also active against Hepatitis B
He should be immunised against Hepatitis B with a normal strength vaccination
He needs ARVs urgently to bring up his CD4 count and his Hepatitis B can be addressed at a later date
explanation:
Hepatitis B is fully suppressed by monotherapy with the ARV drugs, either tenofovir or lamivudine, and minimal resistance has beenreported. Some other NRTIs have partialaction against Hepatitis B and could promote resistance.
This patient has ongoing Hepatitis B as shown by the positive eAb and sAg serology and therefore there is no beneﬁt in vaccination.All HIV positive patients should be offered Hepatitis B vaccination routinely using a double strength vaccination with eithervaccinations at 0, 1 and 6 months or 0, 1, 2 and 12 months.
It is not diﬃcult to include the antiretroviral Tenofovir in and HIV treatment regime, which will address the patient's Hepatitis B. Thepresence of a positive Hepatitis B surface antigen means that the Hepatitis B has not been cleared. A HBV DNA level would bewarranted to fully assess how active the Hepatitis B virus is.

explanation:
Gynaecomastia is one of the less common side effects of efavirenz together with the more common neuropsychiatry side effects.
Abacavir (ABC) is the wrong answer because it does not cause gynaecomastia but causes mainly hypersensitivity reactions andgastrointestinal disturbances.
Lopinavir/ritonavir does not cause gynaecomastia but may cause metabolism abnormalities and gastrointestinal disturbances.
Nevirapine (NVP) is the wrong answer because it does not cause gynaecomastia but causes hypersensitivity reactions andhepatotoxicity as some of its side effects.
Zidovudine (AZT) is the wrong answer because it does not commonly cause gynaecomastia but mainly causes anaemia, neutropeniaand bone marrow suppression as part of its side effects, among others.
Efavirenz is the most common HAART drug associated with gynecomastia.

The patient has many features of septic shock including:Focus of infectionDiarrhoeaDecreased level of consciousnessTachycardia, andHypothermia.

A 26-year-old woman presents with an itchy malodorous yellow vaginal discharge.
On examination, her vulva is erythematous. There is vaginal inﬂammation and punctuate haemorrhages on the cervix. Microscopy of thegenital specimen demonstrates motile ﬂagellated protozoans.
What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
explanation:
This patient has trichomoniasis, an infection caused by Trichomonas vaginalis, a ﬂagellated protozoan.
The incubation period is ﬁve to 28 days.
Clinical features range from being asymptomatic (in most men and 50% of women) to urethritis and vaginitis emphysematosa.
Diagnosis is by dark-ground microscopy of genital wet preps, or culture. Management is a single dose of metronidazole 2 g. It isimportant to treat contacts in order to avoid re-infection.
Metronidazole is relatively contraindicated in the ﬁrst trimester of pregnancy and in such circumstances treatment should bedelayed until the second trimester.
Reference:-
British Association for Sexual Health and HIV (BASHH Guideline for trichomoniasis)

options: Nucleic acid ampliﬁcation technique (NAAT) for Chlamydia
explanation:
NAAT has sensitivities of around 90-95%. It can also run many samples easily.
Cell culture has sensitivities of 60-80% and a lot of expertise is required.
Direct ﬂuorescent antibody (DFA) is labour intensive; it is unsuitable for running large numbers.
Enzyme immunosorbent assay (EIA) has sensitivities of only about 40-70%.
Microimmune ﬂuorescent (micro IF) has a slightly higher sensitivity but is not readily available. It is often used in research settings.

explanation:
Treatment with highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) has been started in the interval between results 1 and results 2.

HAART typically consists of a regime of three or more antiretroviral agents of different classes.

During the consultation he tells you he was diagnosed with HIV ﬁve years ago with a CD4 count of 340 cells/ μ L and that he is currently takingthe antiretrovirals truvada and efavirenz. His HIV was acquired heterosexually. He was started on treatment at diagnosis and has had no otherinfections. He has been stable with a fully suppressed viral load on antiretrovirals ever since. His CD4 count is now 600 cells/ μ L.
How would you manage his illness?
options: Refuse to discuss his HIV and admit directly to infectious diseases unit - only HIV specialists should look after patients with HIV
Discharge with oral amoxicillin but advise rapid contact with his HIV physician as his pneumonia may indicate ARV treatment failure
Admission for treatment with intravenous antibiotics
explanation:
Patients with HIV have a propensity for bronchopneumonia and it is an important clinical indicator for HIV testing.
With an abnormal CD4 count patients with HIV are at risk for invasive streptococcal infection secondary to streptococcalpneumonia. All patients with HIV should have routine pneumococcal vaccination.
In patients with well-controlled HIV and a normal CD4 count pneumonia can be managed as an outpatient using CURB scoring andantimicrobial prescribing guidelines, but with an awareness of the possibility of drug interactions.
His CURB score is 0 and therefore he does not require admission and intravenous ABx. His well-controlled HIV does not effect thisscoring.
Clarithromycin is a CYP3A4 inhibitor and thus should not be used as it has drug interactions with efavirenz. It also has interactionswith nevirapine and protease inhibitors.
Bronchopneumonia does not indicate treatment failure although a patient's HIV physician should be alerted that a pneumonia hasoccurred so they can ensure that the patient is up to date with his pneumococcal and inﬂuenza vaccinations.
General physicians should be able to treat common medical conditions in an HIV patient, so admitting directly to infectious diseasesunit is not appropriate in this case.
